stories.title_en: Using a Horse as Bait to Strip Satin

paragraphs.zh: 江西有陳姓慶名者，常販馬，徃南京承恩寺前，三山街賣。時有一疋銀合好馬，價約值四十金。忽有一棍，擎好傘，穿色衣，翩然而來，佇立瞻顧，不忍舍去。遂問曰：「此馬價賣幾許？」慶曰：「四十兩。」棍曰：「我買，但要歸家作契對銀。」慶問：「何住？」棍曰：「居洪武門。」棍遂騎銀合馬徃，慶亦騎馬随後。行至半途，棍見一緞鋪，即下馬放傘於酒坊邊，囑慶曰：「代看住，待我買緞幾疋，少頃與你同歸。」慶忖：「此人想是富翁，馬諒買得成矣。」棍入緞鋪，故意與之爭價。待緞客以不識價責之，遂佯曰：「我把與一相知者看，即來還價何如？」緞客曰：「有此好物，憑伊與人看，但不可遠去。」棍曰：「我有馬與夥在，更何慮乎？」将緞拿過手，出門便迯去。緞客見馬與夥尚在，心中安然。慶待至午，杳不見來，意必棍徒也。遂舍其傘，騎銀合，又牵一馬囬店。緞客忙奔前，扯住慶曰：「你夥拿吾緞去，你将焉徃？」慶曰：「何人是我夥？」緞客曰：「適間與你同騎馬來者。你何佯推？定要問你取。」慶曰：「那人不知何方鬼，祇是問我買馬，令我同到他家接銀，故與之同來矣。他說在你店買緞，少頃與我同去。我待乆不見來，故騎自馬囬店。你何得妄纏我乎？」緞客曰：「若不是你夥，何�纏我乎？」緞客曰：「若不是你夥，何呌你看傘與馬？我因見你與馬在，始以緞與他。你何通同粧套，脫我緞去？」二人爭辯不伏，扭在應天府理論。緞客以前情直告。慶訴曰：「慶籍江西，販馬為主，常在三山街，翁春店發賣，何嘗作棍？緣遇一人，問我買馬，必要到他家還銀，是以同行。彼中途下馬，在他店拿緞迯去，我亦不知，怎說我是棍之夥？」府尹曰：「不必言，拘店家來問，即見明白。」其店家曰：「慶常販馬，安歇吾家，乃老實本分人也。」緞客曰：「既是老實人，緣何代那棍看傘與馬？此我明白聽見，况他應諾。」慶曰：「呌我看傘，多因為他買馬故也，豈與之同夥？」府尹曰：「那人去，傘亦拿去否？」緞客曰：「未曾拿去。」府尹曰：「此真是棍了。欲脫你緞，故託買馬，以陳慶為質。以他人之馬，賺你之緞，是假道滅虢術也。此你自遭騙，何可罪慶？」各逐出免供。
paragraphs.en: In Jiangxi there was a man surnamed Chen, given name Qing. He often traded horses, going to Nanjing to sell them in front of Cheng'en Temple on Sanshan Street. At that time he had a fine silver-gray horse worth about forty taels. Suddenly a swindler appeared, holding a good umbrella, wearing colorful clothes, coming with an easy air. He stood and gazed, unwilling to leave. He asked, "How much is this horse selling for?" Qing said, "Forty taels." The swindler said, "I'll buy it, but I need to go home to write a deed and match the silver." Qing asked, "Where do you live?" The swindler said, "By Hongwu Gate." The swindler then rode the silver-gray horse off, and Qing also rode a horse following. Halfway there, the swindler saw a satin shop, got off the horse, put his umbrella by a wineshop, and told Qing: "Watch these for me. I'll buy a few bolts of satin, and in a moment we'll go home together." Qing thought: "This man must be rich; surely he can buy the horse." The swindler went into the satin shop and deliberately haggled over the price. When the satin merchant scolded him for not knowing prices, he pretended: "I'll take this to a friend to look at, then come back and settle the price—how about that?" The satin merchant said, "With goods this fine, you may show them to someone, but don't go far." The swindler said, "I have a horse and a companion here—what is there to worry about?" He took the satin in hand, went out the door, and fled. The satin merchant, seeing the horse and companion still there, felt at ease. Qing waited until noon; the man never came back. He realized it must be a swindler. So he left the umbrella, rode the silver-gray horse, and led his other horse back toward the inn. The satin merchant rushed forward, grabbed Qing, and said, "Your companion took my satin—where are you going?" Qing said, "Who is my companion?" The satin merchant said, "The one who just now rode here with you. Why pretend? I must get it from you." Qing said, "That man is some unknown devil. He only asked to buy my horse and told me to go with him to his house for the silver, so I came with him. He said he would buy satin at your shop and go with me in a moment. I waited a long time and he didn't come, so I rode my own horse back to the inn. How can you pester me for no reason?" The satin merchant said, "If he wasn't your partner, why did he tell you to watch the umbrella and horse? I only gave him the satin because I saw you and the horse here. How can you two collude in a setup and strip me of my satin?" The two argued without yielding and dragged each other to Yingtian Prefecture to argue the case. The satin merchant told the facts as above. Qing pleaded: "I am registered in Jiangxi; my main business is selling horses. I often sell at Sanshan Street, at Weng Chun's inn. When have I ever been a swindler? I happened to meet a man who asked to buy my horse and insisted on going to his house to pay, so I went with him. Midway he got off the horse, took satin from this man's shop, and fled. I didn't know—how can you say I am the swindler's partner?" The prefect said, "No need to argue. Bring the innkeeper and it will be clear." The innkeeper said, "Qing often trades horses and stays at my place; he is an honest, decent man." The satin merchant said, "If he is honest, why did he watch the umbrella and horse for that swindler? I clearly heard this, and he agreed." Qing said, "He asked me to watch the umbrella because he was buying my horse—how does that make me his partner?" The prefect said, "When that man left, did he take the umbrella too?" The satin merchant said, "He did not." The prefect said, "This truly is a swindler. He wanted to strip you of your satin, so he pretended to buy a horse and used Chen Qing as security. Using another man's horse to cheat you of your satin is the 'borrow a path to destroy Guo' trick. You brought this swindle on yourself—how can you blame Qing?" Each was dismissed without further testimony.

paragraphs.zh: 吾觀作棍亦多術矣。言買馬，非買馬，實欲假馬作囮，為脫緞之術。故先以色服章身，令人信其為真豪富；既而佇立相馬，令人信其為真作家；迨入緞鋪，誑言有馬與夥，令人信其為真實言；至脫緞而走，以一傘貽慶，與緞客爭訟：此皆以巧術愚弄人也。若非府尹明察，断其為假道滅虢，則行人得牛，不幾邑人之災乎？雖然慶未至混跡於縲絏，緞客已被鬼迷於白晝矣。小人之計甚詭，君子之防宜密。庶棍術雖多，亦不能愚弄我也。
paragraphs.en: Note: I observe that swindlers have many tricks. He said he was buying a horse, but he was not buying a horse; he really wanted to use the horse as a decoy, as a method to strip satin. First he dressed in colorful clothes, making people believe he was truly wealthy; then he stood gazing at the horse, making people believe he was a true judge of horseflesh; then he entered the satin shop and lied that he had a horse and a companion, making people believe his words were true; after stripping the satin and fleeing, he left one umbrella with Qing, so Qing and the satin merchant would go to court: all this was using clever tricks to fool people. If the prefect had not seen clearly and judged it as "borrowing a path to destroy Guo," then when a traveler gets an ox, would it not nearly become a disaster for the townsman? Although Qing did not end up mixed into fetters, the satin merchant had already been bewitched in broad daylight. A petty man's schemes are very crafty; a gentleman's defenses should be tight. Then even if swindlers have many tricks, they cannot fool me.

stories.title_en: First Entrusting Silver, Then Running Off

paragraphs.zh: 通州有姓蘇名廣者，同一子販松江梭布，徃福建賣。布銀入手，囬至半途，遇一人姓紀名勝，自稱同府異縣，鄉語相同，亦在福建賣布而歸。勝乃雛家，途中認廣為親鄉里，見廣財本更多，乃以己銀貳拾餘兩寄藏於蘇廣箱内。一路小心代劳，渾如同伴。後至日乆，勝見利而生姦。一夜，佯稱瀉病，連起開門出去数次。不知廣乃老客也，見其開門徃返，疑彼有詐謀；且其來歷不明，「彼雖有銀貳拾餘兩寄我箱内，今夜似有歹意。」乗其出，即潛起來，将己銀與紀勝銀并實落衣物另藏别包袱，置在己身邊；仍以舊衣被包数片磚石放在原箱内，佯作熟睡。勝察廣父子都睡去，将廣銀箱夤夜挑走。廣在床聽勝動静，出門不歸，曰：「此果棍也，非我，險遭此脫迯矣。」次日，廣起，故驚訝勝竊他銀本，将店主扭打，說他通同将我銀偷去。其子弗知父之謀，尤怒歐不已。父密謂曰：「此事我已如此如此。」方止。早飯後，廣曰：「我徃縣告，若捕得那棍，你來作證；不然，定要問你取矣。」廣知勝反中己術，徑從小路潛歸。勝自幸竊得廣銀，茫茫然行至午，路将百里。開其箱，内乃磚石、舊衣也。頓足大恨，復囬原店。却被店主扭打一場，大罵曰：「這賊！你偷人銀，致我被累！」将绳繫頸，欲要送官。隻得吐出真情，叩頭懇免。時勝與廣已隔数日程途，追之不及，徒自悔恨而已。
paragraphs.en: In Tongzhou there was a man named Su Guang who, with one son, traded Songjiang shuttle cloth, going to Fujian to sell it. After getting the cloth-silver in hand, on the way back they met a man named Ji Sheng, who claimed to be from the same prefecture but a different county, with the same local dialect, also returning from selling cloth in Fujian. Sheng was a novice in the trade. On the road he treated Guang as a fellow townsman; seeing that Guang had more capital, he entrusted more than twenty taels of his own silver to be stored in Su Guang's chest. All along the way he was careful and helpful, just like a companion. After many days, Sheng saw profit and grew crooked. One night he pretended to have diarrhea, getting up and opening the door to go out several times. He did not know Guang was an old hand. Seeing him open the door and go back and forth, Guang suspected a plot; and his background was unclear. "Though he has more than twenty taels stored in my chest, tonight he seems to have ill intent." While Sheng was out, Guang quietly got up, took his own silver and Ji Sheng's silver together with the real clothes and goods, hid them in another bundle, and kept it by his side; he still packed the old clothes and bedding with several bricks and stones in the original chest, and pretended to sleep soundly. Sheng, seeing that Guang and his son were both asleep, carried off Guang's silver chest in the night. Guang in bed listened to Sheng's movements; when he went out and did not return, he said, "This really is a swindler. If it weren't for me, we would have nearly been stripped and left empty." The next day Guang got up, pretended to be shocked that Sheng had stolen his silver capital, grabbed the innkeeper and beat him, saying he had colluded to steal his silver. His son did not know his father's plan and was even more furious, beating without stopping. The father secretly told him, "I have already done such-and-such about this." Only then did he stop. After breakfast, Guang said, "I'm going to the county to file a complaint. If they catch that swindler, you come as witness; otherwise I'll certainly demand it from you." Guang knew Sheng had fallen into his own trick, and quietly went home by a side path. Sheng congratulated himself on stealing Guang's silver, wandering until noon, nearly a hundred li. He opened the chest: inside were bricks, stones, and old clothes. He stamped his feet in great hatred and went back to the original inn. But he was grabbed and beaten by the innkeeper, who cursed: "You thief! You stole someone's silver and got me implicated!" He put a rope around Sheng's neck, wanting to send him to the officials. Sheng had no choice but to confess the truth and kowtow begging to be spared. By then Sheng and Guang were already several days' journey apart; he could not catch up, and could only regret it himself.

paragraphs.zh: 按：紀勝非雛客，乃雛棍也。先将己銀託寄於廣，令其不疑；後以詐瀉開門，候其熟睡，即連彼銀共竊而迯。彼之為計，亦甚巧矣。盖此乃「欲取姑與」，棍局中一甜術也。孰知廣乃老客，見出其上，察其動静，已照其肝胆。故因機乗機，将計就計，勝已入厥筭中而不自知矣。夫勝欲利人之有，反自喪其有，雛家光棍，又不如老年江湖也。待後囬店，被其扭打，捻頸哀告以求免，是自貽伊戚，又誰咎也？天理昭昭，此足為鑑。
paragraphs.en: Note: Ji Sheng was not a novice merchant, but a novice swindler. First he entrusted his own silver to Guang, so Guang would not suspect; then he pretended diarrhea to open the door, waited until they were sound asleep, and stole both their silver and fled. His plan was quite clever. This is "give in order to take"—a sweet trick among swindler schemes. Who knew Guang was an old traveler, saw through it, watched his movements, and already understood his insides. So he used the opportunity, turned the scheme back, and Sheng had already entered his calculations without knowing it. Sheng wanted to profit from another's goods and instead lost his own. A novice swindler is no match for an old hand of the rivers and lakes. Later when he returned to the inn, he was grabbed and beaten, had his neck twisted, and begged to be spared—he brought this trouble on himself; who else is to blame? Heaven's principle is clear; this is enough to serve as a warning.

paragraphs.zh: 福建建陽人鄧招寶者，常以挑販為生。一日，販小猪四隻，徃崇安、大安去賣。行至馬安嶺上，遇一棍問他買猪。寶意此山徑僻嶺，無人徃來，人家又遠，何此人在路上買猪？疑之，因問其何住。棍曰：「既前馬安坪也。」寶曰：「既要買，我同你家去。」棍曰：「我要徃縣。你拿出與我看，若合吾意，議定價方好囬家秤銀；不然，恐阻程途矣。」此棍言之近理，寶即然之，遂拿一猪與看。棍接過手，拿住猪尾放地上細看，乃故放手，致猪便走。佯作驚恐状曰：「差矣，差矣！」即忙趕捉——不知趕之正驱之也。寶見猪遠走，猛心奔前追捉，豈知已墮其術也。棍見寶趕猪，約離籠二三百步，即旋於籠内拿一猪在手，又踢倒二籠，猪俱迯出，大聲曰：「多謝你！慢慢尋！」寶欲趕棍，三猪出籠迯走，恐因此而失彼；况棍走遠難追，但呪罵一場。幸得三猪成聚，收拾入籠，抱恨而去。
paragraphs.en: Deng Zhaobao of Jianyang, Fujian, often made a living as a porter-peddler. One day he was taking four piglets to Chong'an and Da'an to sell. On Ma'an Ridge he met a swindler who asked to buy pigs. Bao thought: this mountain path is remote, no one comes and goes, houses are far away—why would this man buy pigs on the road? He was suspicious, so he asked where the man lived. The swindler said, "Just ahead, at Ma'anping." Bao said, "If you want to buy, I'll go with you to your house." The swindler said, "I have to go to the county seat. You take one out for me to look at. If it suits me, we'll settle the price and then I can go home to weigh out the silver; otherwise I'm afraid it will delay my journey." The swindler's words seemed reasonable, so Bao agreed and took out one pig to show. The swindler took it, held the pig's tail and set it on the ground to look closely, then deliberately let go so the pig ran off. He pretended to be startled: "Oh no, oh no!" and hurriedly chased it—not knowing that chasing it was exactly driving it away. Bao saw the pig running far and dashed forward to catch it, not knowing he had already fallen into the trap. When the swindler saw Bao chasing the pig, about two or three hundred paces from the cages, he quickly took one pig from a cage, kicked over the other two cages so the pigs all ran out, and shouted, "Thanks! Take your time looking!" Bao wanted to chase the swindler, but three pigs had run from the cages; he feared losing those while chasing this. Besides, the swindler had gone too far to catch. He could only curse. Luckily the three pigs gathered together; he put them back in the cages and left in resentment.

paragraphs.zh: 吾觀棍之脫猪也，一邂逅相逢之頃，賊念即生，乃以詭言相哄，致寶深信，所謂「君子可欺以其方」者也。乃始也放猪佯逐，以误其遠趕之於前；繼也擒猪踢籠，以制其不趕之於後：使人明墮其術而不自知。倉卒粧套，抑何譎也！商者鑑此！勿謂暗機隱械，宜為慎防；即明圈顯套，尤當加謹。
paragraphs.en: Note: I observe how the swindler stripped him of a pig. In the moment of a chance meeting, a thief's thought arose; he used deceitful words to fool Bao, so Bao deeply believed him—this is what is meant by "a gentleman can be deceived by what seems reasonable." First he let a pig go and pretended to chase it, to mislead Bao into chasing far ahead; then he seized a pig and kicked the cages, so Bao could not chase afterward: making a man fall openly into the trick without knowing it. A setup made in haste—how crafty! Merchants, take this as a warning! Do not say only hidden mechanisms need careful defense; even open traps and obvious setups should be guarded against all the more.

stories.title_en: Meeting the Village Head and Stripping a Teapot Instead

paragraphs.zh: 趙通，延平府南平縣人也。家世積善，錢糧頗多，差當七啚一甲裡役。其甲首林錢一者，機智過人，不務生理，第飲賭宿娼，後來家業消條，無處栖身，隻得迯外。通亦不知其向徃。一日，通與僕徃杭貿易，經過浦城，憩息於亭，�僕徃杭貿易，經過浦城，憩息於亭，遆見錢一。通遂罵之曰：「這奴才！你迯外数年，户丁不納，糧差累賠，是何理也？今你見我，你何以說？」錢一被罵不甘，心生一計，向前賠笑曰：「我每欲囬，送條編與里長，奈我家中欠人財物甚多，難以抵償，故不敢囬矣。今幸遇里長，如天降下，敢再推辭？况這幾年賴里長福庇，開店西關码頭，家中稍裕。新娶邑人徐某之妾為妻，被人欺姦。我乃孤身一人，出外獨居，無奈伊何！今幸遇里長，則有主矣。里長徃杭州，亦經門處過，即到我家暫歇，自當筭還編銀；又煩代我作主。」通聽其言，私心喜曰：「今日得此，可作徃杭盤費，誠可謂出門招財也。」遂與同行。至一店所，錢曰：「里長今朝起早，又路行半日，肚又飢矣，上店沽酒濕口何如？」應曰：「可。」遂入店，呌店主煖酒、切豆腐，與通食。更問店主曰：「這裡有好紅酒、猪肉否？」店主曰：「市前游店肉酒俱有。」錢一曰：「可借壺、秤一用。」店主拿壺、秤出，錢接過手，直望游店轉轉抹角潛躲而去。通與僕吃酒，一壺将盡，乃對僕曰：「錢一去許乆不來，莫非與人爭闘？不然，此時當來矣。汝徃看之。」僕即徃酒肉店去問，說并無錢一。待欲尋他，又不知他去向，隻得秤銀還酒。店主收銀，索取壺、秤。通怒曰：「酒是我吃，我還你猶可；壺、秤是你自交錢一，何干我事？」店主曰：「人同你來，你在我店飲酒，故把壺、秤借他。不然，我曉得甚么錢一？」言來言去，兩下角口大鬧。眾人來勸，問其來歷，始知甲首騙里長入店，更脫店主壺、秤。眾大笑曰：「是他自錯，賠他也罷。」不得已代賠，嘔氣抱忿而去。
paragraphs.en: Zhao Tong was a man of Nanping County, Yanping Prefecture. His family had long done good deeds, had quite a lot of tax-grain, and he served as lizhang (village head) of Jia One in Tu Seven. One of his jia-heads, Lin Qianyi, was extremely clever, did not attend to a proper livelihood, only drank, gambled, and visited prostitutes. Later his household declined; he had nowhere to live and could only flee abroad. Tong did not know where he had gone. One day Tong and a servant went to Hangzhou to trade. Passing Pucheng, they rested at a pavilion and unexpectedly saw Qianyi. Tong then scolded him: "You slave! You've been away for years, the household men don't pay, I've had to make up the grain and corvée—what sense is that? Now you see me, what do you say?" Qianyi, unwilling to take the scolding, thought of a plan, came forward with an apologetic smile: "I always wanted to return and deliver the combined tax to the lizhang, but my family owes people a great deal and I cannot pay, so I dared not go back. Now I'm lucky to meet the lizhang, as if heaven sent you—how could I refuse again? Besides, these few years, thanks to the lizhang's blessing, I opened a shop at the Xiguan wharf and my household is somewhat comfortable. I newly took a certain Xu's concubine of this town as wife; someone has been bullying her and committing adultery. I am a lone man living abroad, and can do nothing about it! Now that I meet the lizhang, I have a master. The lizhang going to Hangzhou also passes my door; just stop at my house a while, I will of course calculate and repay the tax silver; and I trouble you to take my part." Tong heard this and privately rejoiced: "Getting this today can serve as traveling money to Hangzhou; truly, leaving home invites wealth." So they went together. At a shop, Qianyi said, "The lizhang started early today and has walked half a day; you're hungry—how about going into a shop for some wine to wet the mouth?" Tong said, "Fine." They went in; Qianyi called the shopkeeper to warm wine and slice tofu for Tong to eat. He further asked the shopkeeper, "Is there good red wine and pork here?" The shopkeeper said, "The You shop in front of the market has both meat and wine." Qianyi said, "May I borrow a pot and a scale?" The shopkeeper brought out a pot and scale; Qianyi took them, headed toward the You shop, turned corners, and slipped away. Tong and the servant drank; one pot was nearly empty. Tong said to the servant, "Qianyi has been gone a long time—could he be fighting someone? Otherwise he should have come by now. Go look." The servant went to the wine-and-meat shop and asked; they said there was no Qianyi. He wanted to search but did not know where he had gone, so they could only weigh out silver to pay for the wine. The shopkeeper took the silver and demanded the pot and scale. Tong angrily said, "I drank the wine, so I can pay you; the pot and scale you yourself handed to Qianyi—what has that to do with me?" The shopkeeper said, "The man came with you; you were drinking in my shop, so I lent him the pot and scale. Otherwise, what do I know of any Qianyi?" Words went back and forth; they quarreled loudly. People came to mediate, asked about the background, and then learned that a jia-head had lured the lizhang into a shop and also stripped the shopkeeper of pot and scale. Everyone laughed: "It was his own mistake; just compensate him." Tong had no choice but to pay, and left choking with anger.

paragraphs.zh: 按：林錢一始說家頗充裕，妻被棍姦，欲投里長作主，致人不疑；繼也入店，借壺、秤沽酒肉，以叙間濶之情，使人不備：玩通於股掌之中，術亦巧矣。然錢一狡猾有素，通亦知之，乃一卒遇之，通遂信其言而入店飲酒；更欲沽紅買肉，皆非欵待之真情。在通當燭其偽而止之曰：「店中不便，有酒有肉，到家食之未晚也。」則錢一姦無所施。将道旁脫走不暇，何至賠壺、秤而受嘔氣也？故錢一狡也，而通亦欠檢點焉。嘻！
paragraphs.en: Note: Lin Qianyi first said his household was fairly well off, his wife had been seduced by a swindler, and he wanted the lizhang to take his part, so no one would suspect; then he went into a shop, borrowed pot and scale to buy wine and meat, to talk over old times and make people unprepared: he played with Tong in the palm of his hand—the trick was clever. Yet Qianyi had long been cunning, and Tong knew it; but on a sudden meeting, Tong believed his words and went into a shop to drink; wanting red wine and meat was not true hospitality. Tong should have seen through the falsehood and stopped him: "The shop is inconvenient; if there is wine and meat, we'll eat at your house, it's not too late." Then Qianyi would have had nowhere to work his scheme. He would have been too busy fleeing by the roadside—how would it have come to paying for pot and scale and swallowing anger? So Qianyi was cunning, but Tong also lacked caution. Alas!

stories.title_en: Stealing Shop Cloth Openly in the Bustle

paragraphs.zh: 吴勝理，徽州府休寧縣人，在蘇州府開鋪，收買各樣色布，揭行生意最大，四方買者極多，每日有幾十兩銀交易。外開鋪面，裡藏各貨。一日，有幾夥客人凑集買布，皆在内堂作帐對銀。一棍乗其叢雜，亦在鋪呌買布。勝理出於施礼，待茶畢，安頓外鋪少坐。勝理復入内，與前客對銀。其棍蓦其鋪無守者，故近門邊，詐拱揖相辭状，遂近鋪邊拿布一捆，拖在肩上，缓步行去。雖對鋪者，亦不覺其盗。後内堂诸商交易畢，勝理送客出外，忽不見鋪上布，問對門店人曰：「我鋪裡一捆布是何人拿去？」對門店人曰：「你�鋪裡一捆布是何人拿去？」對門店人曰：「你遆間後來那客人，與你拱手作辭，方拖布去，眾皆見之，你何佯失布？」勝理曰：「因内忙，故安他在外鋪坐，候前客事畢，然後與他作帐。何曾賣布與他？」鄰人訝曰：「狡哉，此棍！彼佯拱手相辭，令我辈不敢說他是賊，缓步而行，明白脫去矣！将奈何？」勝理隻得懊恨一場而罷。
paragraphs.en: Wu Shengli, a man of Xiuning County, Huizhou Prefecture, opened a shop in Suzhou Prefecture, buying all kinds of colored cloth. His wholesale business was the largest; buyers from all quarters were extremely many; every day there were tens of taels of silver in trade. Outside he opened a shop front; inside he stored various goods. One day several groups of customers gathered to buy cloth, all in the inner hall making accounts and matching silver. A swindler, taking advantage of the crowd, also called out in the shop to buy cloth. Shengli came out, bowed, served tea, and seated him in the outer shop to sit a while. Shengli went back inside to match silver with the earlier customers. The swindler, seeing no one watching the shop, approached the doorway, pretended to cup his hands in farewell, then went to the shop side, took a bundle of cloth, slung it on his shoulder, and walked slowly away. Even the people across the street did not notice it was theft. Later when the merchants in the inner hall finished their deals, Shengli saw the customers out, suddenly found the shop cloth gone, and asked the people opposite: "Who took a bundle of cloth from my shop?" The people opposite said, "That customer who came later just now cupped his hands to take leave of you and then dragged the cloth away. Everyone saw it—why pretend you've lost cloth?" Shengli said, "Because I was busy inside, I seated him in the outer shop to wait until the earlier customers were done, then make an account with him. When did I ever sell him cloth?" The neighbors marveled: "Crafty, this swindler! He pretended to cup his hands in farewell so we wouldn't dare say he was a thief, walked slowly, and openly stripped it away! What can be done?" Shengli could only regret it and let it go.

paragraphs.zh: 按：棍之竊斯布也，初須乗其叢雜，入其店中，尚未定其騙局之所出也。至勝理待其茶而安之外鋪少坐，左顧右盼而姦謀遂决矣。故拱揖而辭，而明拖其布，如荆州之暗袭，不甚費力，真可謂高手矣。在勝理，店積貨物，宜不離看守，方可保無虞。關防不密，安知無棍徒混入行姦乎？待布既失而後扼腕，何益哉？大凡坐鋪者，當知此而謹慎之可也。
paragraphs.en: Note: When the swindler stole this cloth, at first he had to take advantage of the crowd and enter the shop; he had not yet decided how the swindle would come out. When Shengli served him tea and seated him in the outer shop a while, he looked left and right and then the crooked plan was decided. So he cupped his hands in farewell and openly dragged the cloth, like a stealth attack on Jingzhou, without much effort—truly a high hand. As for Shengli, with goods piled in the shop, he should not have left them unwatched, so as to keep them safe. If the watch is not tight, how can one know no swindlers will mix in and work their schemes? After the cloth is lost, wringing one's wrists—what good is that? In general, those who sit in shops should know this and be careful.

stories.title_en: Pretending to Steal a Goose to Strip Blue Cloth

paragraphs.zh: 有一大鋪，布匹極多，交易叢雜，隻自己一人看店。其店之對門人，養一圈鹅，鸣聲嘈雜。開鋪者惡其聒耳，尝曰：「此惡物何無盗之者？與我耳頭得沉静些。」忽棍聞之。一日，乗其店中閑寂，遂入店拱手，以手按柜頭一捆青布，輕輕言曰：「不敢相瞒，我實是一小偷，愛得對門店下一隻鹅吃，隻大街面難下手。我有一小術，祇要一个人贊成。」店主曰：「如何贊成？」小偷曰：「我在這邊問曰：『可拿去否？』汝在内高聲應曰：『可。』又再問曰：『我真拿去？』汝再應曰：『說定了，任從拿去。』我便去拿，方掩得路人耳目。託你贊成，後日你家不須閉門，亦無賊入矣。但你須在内去，莫得竊視，視則法不灵。你直聽鹅聲息，我事方畢，你可出來。」店主然之。小偷高聲問曰：「我拿去否？」内高聲應曰：「憑你拿去。」又再高聲問曰：「我真拿去？」内又高聲應曰：「說定了，任你拿去。」兩旁店人皆聞其問答之語，小偷遂負其柜上一捆青布而去——人以為借去也。其店主在内，聽得鹅聲，不敢出來。其盗布者匆匆行之乆矣。待之多時，鹅聲不绝。其店主恐店内乆無人守，隻得外出。看鹅尚在，自己柜頭反失一捆青布。顧問兩旁店曰：「遆才誰上我店，拿我一捆布去？」左右店皆答曰：「是那个問你買的，你再三應聲，呌他祇管拿去。今拿去已乆矣。」店主抚心自悔曰：「我明被此人騙了！祇是自己皆死，說不得也。」事乆，眾鄰覺之，始笑此人之痴，而深服此棍賊之高手矣。
paragraphs.en: There was a large shop with a great many bolts of cloth, trade crowded and mixed, with only the owner himself watching the shop. The person across the street kept a pen of geese, whose honking was noisy. The shopkeeper hated the noise and once said, "Why has no one stolen these wretched creatures? Then my ears would get some quiet." A swindler happened to hear this. One day, when the shop was idle and quiet, he went in, cupped his hands, pressed his hand on a bundle of blue cloth on the counter, and said softly, "I won't hide it from you: I am really a petty thief. I'd love to eat one of the geese under the shop across the way, but it's a main street and hard to make a move. I have a small trick; I just need one person to play along." The shopkeeper said, "How play along?" The thief said, "I'll ask from here: 'May I take it?' You answer loudly from inside: 'Yes.' I'll ask again: 'I'm really taking it?' You answer again: 'It's settled; take it as you please.' Then I'll go take it, and that will cover the ears and eyes of people on the road. If you help me, later your house won't need to shut the door and no thief will enter. But you must go inside; don't peek—if you look, the method won't work. Just listen until the goose-sounds stop; when I'm done, you can come out." The shopkeeper agreed. The thief asked loudly, "May I take it?" From inside came a loud answer: "Take it as you please." He asked again loudly, "I'm really taking it?" From inside again: "It's settled; take it as you please." The shops on both sides all heard this question and answer. The thief then shouldered a bundle of blue cloth from the counter and left—people thought it was borrowed. The shopkeeper inside, hearing goose-sounds, dared not come out. The cloth-thief had already hurried off long ago. After waiting a long time, the goose-sounds did not stop. The shopkeeper feared the shop would be unwatched too long and had to go out. He saw the geese still there, and a bundle of blue cloth missing from his own counter. He asked the shops on both sides: "Just now who came into my shop and took a bundle of my cloth?" The shops left and right all answered: "It was that one who asked to buy from you. You answered again and again, telling him to just take it. He's been gone a long time." The shopkeeper beat his breast and regretted: "I've clearly been swindled by this man! It's all my own death; I can't even speak of it." After a long time the neighbors figured it out; they began to laugh at this man's folly and deeply admire the swindler-thief's high skill.

paragraphs.zh: 按：君子仁民愛物，而仁之先施者，莫如鄰；物之愛者，即鹅亦居其一。何對鄰人養鹅，惡在嘈雜之聲，必欲盗之者以殺之，愛物之謂何哉？利失對鄰之鹅，而贊成棍賊以盗之，仁心安在？是以致使棍聞其言，乗機而行竊，反贊成其偷，亦是鼠辈也。欲去人之鹅，而反自失其布，是自貽祸也，将誰怨哉？若能仁以處鄰，而量足以容物，何至有此失也！
paragraphs.en: Note: A gentleman is kind to people and loves living things; the first to receive kindness should be neighbors; among things to love, even geese are one. Why, when a neighbor keeps geese, hate the noisy sound and wish a thief would kill them—what kind of love for living things is that? He wanted to lose the neighbor's geese and agreed to help a swindler-thief steal them—where is the humane heart? So when a swindler heard his words and seized the chance to steal, and he even helped the theft, he too was a rat. He wanted to get rid of another's geese and instead lost his own cloth; he brought disaster on himself—whom can he blame? If he had treated neighbors with kindness and had enough measure to tolerate things, how would he have come to this loss?

stories.title_en: Using Another Man's House to Strip a Customer's Cloth

paragraphs.zh: 聂道應，别号西湖，邵武六都人。家原富厚，住屋宏深。後因訟耗家，以裁缝為業。忽一日徃人家裁衣。有一光棍見客人賣布，知應出外，故领到應家前栋坐定，竟入内堂，私問應妻云：「汝丈夫在家否？」其妻曰：「徃前村裁衣。」棍曰：「我要造数件衣服，今日歸否？」對曰：「要明日歸。」棍曰：「我有同伴在你前栋坐，口渴，求茶一杯吃。」應妻即討茶二杯，放於斫凳上。棍将茶捧與布客飲。飲罷，接杯入，方出拣布四匹，還銀壹兩，隻銀不成色。客曰：「此價要換好銀。」棍曰：「我儿子為人裁衣，待明日歸換與你。」言未畢，棍预套一人來問：「針工在家否？」棍應曰：「要明日歸。」其人即去。布客曰：「你收起布，明日換之與我。」客既出，少頃棍亦拖布迯去。次早，布客到應家問曰：「針工歸否？」應妻曰：「午後囬。」布客次早又問：「針工歸否？」應妻又曰：「今午囬。」布客午後又來問，應妻曰：「未歸。」布客怒曰：「你公公前日拿布四匹，說要針工歸來還銀，何再三推託？你公公何去？」應妻道：「這客人好胡說！我家哪有公公？誰人拿你布？」二人角口大鬧。鄰人辯曰：「他何曾有公公？况其丈夫又不在家，你布不知何人拿去，安可妄取？」布客無奈，状投署印同知钟爷。状准，即拘四鄰來审。眾云：「應不在家，况父已死。其布不知甚人脫去。」钟爷曰：「布在他家脫去，那日何人到他家下？着鄰約為之穷究，必有着落矣。」鄰約不能究，乃勸西湖曰：「令正不合被棍脫茶，致误客人以布付棍，當認一半；布客不合輕易以布付人，亦當自認一半。」二家諾然，依此囬報。钟爷以鄰約處得明白，俱各免供。
paragraphs.en: Nie Daoying, courtesy name Xihu, was a man of Liudu, Shaowu. His family had originally been wealthy, with a large, deep house. Later lawsuits wasted the household; he made a living as a tailor. One day he went to someone's house to cut clothes. A swindler saw a customer selling cloth, knew Ying was out, so he led the man to sit in Ying's front hall, then went into the inner rooms and privately asked Ying's wife: "Is your husband home?" The wife said, "He's gone to the next village to cut clothes." The swindler said, "I need several garments made. Will he be back today?" She said, "He'll be back tomorrow." The swindler said, "I have a companion sitting in your front hall, thirsty; may I ask for a cup of tea?" Ying's wife then fetched two cups of tea and put them on the chopping-stool. The swindler carried the tea to the cloth merchant to drink. After drinking, he took the cups back in, then came out, picked four bolts of cloth, and paid one tael of silver—but the silver was not of good quality. The customer said, "At this price I need it exchanged for good silver." The swindler said, "My son is cutting clothes for people; when he returns tomorrow I'll exchange it for you." Before he finished speaking, a man the swindler had already planted came to ask: "Is the needle-worker home?" The swindler answered, "He'll be back tomorrow." That man left. The cloth merchant said, "You put the cloth away; tomorrow exchange it for me." After the customer left, in a moment the swindler also dragged the cloth and fled. The next morning the cloth merchant came to Ying's house and asked, "Has the needle-worker returned?" Ying's wife said, "This afternoon." The next morning the cloth merchant asked again, "Has the needle-worker returned?" Ying's wife said again, "This noon." In the afternoon the cloth merchant came again; Ying's wife said, "Not back yet." The cloth merchant angrily said, "Your father-in-law the other day took four bolts of cloth, saying he'd wait for the needle-worker to return to pay silver—why keep putting it off? Where has your father-in-law gone?" Ying's wife said, "This customer talks nonsense! What father-in-law do we have? Who took your cloth?" The two quarreled loudly. Neighbors argued: "When did he ever have a father-in-law? Besides, her husband isn't home. We don't know who took your cloth—how can you demand it wrongly?" The cloth merchant had no choice and filed a complaint with Acting Vice Prefect Zhong. The complaint was accepted; the four neighbors were summoned for questioning. All said: "Ying was not home, and his father is already dead. We don't know who stripped the cloth." Master Zhong said, "The cloth was stripped at his house. Who came to his house that day? Have the neighborhood compact investigate thoroughly; there must be a trail." The neighborhood compact could not investigate, so they advised Xihu: "Your wife should not have been stripped of tea by the swindler, causing the customer to hand cloth to the swindler; you should take half the loss. The cloth merchant should not have lightly handed cloth to someone; he should also take half." Both families agreed and reported back. Master Zhong, seeing the neighborhood compact had settled it clearly, dismissed both without further testimony.

paragraphs.zh: 按：布入人家賣，又飲人家之茶，則買主似有着落矣，誰不肯以布與之？詎料此棍借其屋，賺其茶，以為脫布之媒；又還其銀，止爭銀色而許換，誰知防之？今後交易，惟兩相交付。彼雖許換銀，布隻抱去，明日重來，則無受脫之事矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: When cloth is sold into someone's house, and one drinks that house's tea, the buyer seems to have a footing—who would not hand over the cloth? Who would have thought this swindler borrowed the house and cheated them of tea as a medium to strip cloth; and he even paid silver, only arguing about the silver's quality and promising to exchange it—who would know to guard against it? From now on in trade, only exchange both sides at once. Even if he promises to exchange the silver, just take the cloth away and come back tomorrow—then there will be no being stripped.

stories.title_en: Posing as a Carpenter to Carry Off a Money Table

paragraphs.zh: 建寧府凡換錢者，皆以一椅一桌厨列於街上，置錢於桌，以待人換。午則歸家食飯，晚則收起錢，以桌厨寄附近人家。明日復然。有一人桌厨内約積有錢五六千，其桌破坏一角。旁有一棍，看此破桌厨内多錢，心生一計。待此人起身食午，即粧做一木匠，以手巾缚腰，插一利斧於旁，手拿六尺，将此桌厨横量直量一次，高聲自說自應曰：「這樣破东西，當做一新的來換，反呌我修补，怎么修得？真是吝啬的人！」自說了一場。一手拿六尺，将桌厨錢輕輕侧倾作一邊，将桌厨負在無人處，以斧砍開，取錢而迯。時旁人都道是換錢的呌木匠拿去修，那料大眾人群中，有棍敢脫此也。乃午後，換錢者到，問旁人曰：「我桌厨哪裡去？」眾合答曰：「你呌木匠拿去修，匠還說你吝啬，何不再做新的，乃修此破物？彼已負去修矣。」換錢者曰：「我并未呌匠來，此是光棍脫去。」急沿途而访問，見空僻處桌厨剖破，錢無一文，怅恨而歸。
paragraphs.en: In Jianning Prefecture, all money-changers set a chair and a table-cabinet on the street, put coins on the table, and waited for people to exchange. At noon they went home to eat; in the evening they collected the coins and left the table-cabinet with a nearby household. The next day they did the same. One man had about five or six thousand coins accumulated in his table-cabinet; a corner of the table was broken. A swindler nearby, seeing much money in this broken table-cabinet, thought of a plan. When the man got up to eat lunch, he dressed as a carpenter, tied a towel around his waist, stuck a sharp axe at his side, held a six-foot measuring stick, measured the table-cabinet this way and that, and said loudly to himself: "Something this broken—they should have a new one made to replace it, yet they tell me to patch it—how can it be patched? Truly a stingy man!" After talking to himself, with one hand holding the six-foot stick, he gently tipped the coins in the table-cabinet to one side, hoisted the table-cabinet onto his back, carried it to a deserted place, chopped it open with the axe, took the coins, and fled. At the time bystanders all thought the money-changer had called a carpenter to take it for repair; who would have thought that in a crowd there was a swindler bold enough to strip this. In the afternoon the money-changer arrived and asked bystanders, "Where has my table-cabinet gone?" They all answered: "You called a carpenter to take it for repair. The carpenter even said you were stingy—why not make a new one instead of repairing this broken thing? He's already carried it off to repair." The money-changer said, "I never called a carpenter; this is a swindler who stripped it." He hurriedly asked along the road, found the table-cabinet chopped open in a deserted place, not a single coin left, and returned in despair.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍粧匠而來，大舉大動，大志大言，人哪知他是脫？祇匠人修舊物，須在作場内，何須帶斧帶六尺而來？粧為匠便非匠矣。但他人物件，他人為修，何人替他盤詰？此棍所以得行其詐也。然因此以推其餘，凡來歷不明而粧情甚肖者，倍宜加察也。
paragraphs.en: Note: This swindler came dressed as a carpenter, making a big show, big movements, big talk—who would know he was stripping? But a carpenter repairing old things should do it in the workshop; why bring an axe and a six-foot stick? Dressing as a carpenter already meant he was not a carpenter. But it was another man's object, another man supposedly repairing it—who would interrogate on his behalf? That is how this swindler could work his fraud. From this we can infer the rest: whenever someone's background is unclear and the act is very convincing, one should examine twice as carefully.
